Atlas/Biology/Cells & organisation

Biology · Cells & organisation · ABOUT 20 MINUTES

How do tiny cells keep a whole body going?

A heart looks like one solid object, but it contains living cells doing different jobs. Cells are the basic units of life; organisation connects their small-scale work to what a whole organism can do.

START WITH A QUESTION

Imagine a heart made entirely of muscle cells, with no other kinds of cell. Would being able to squeeze be enough to make it a working pump? Predict what might be missing.

Have a guess together before revealing the idea.

The idea underneath +

In a many-celled organism, specialised cells have structures suited to particular jobs. Groups of cells working together form tissues. Different tissues combine into organs, such as the heart; organs cooperate in systems, such as the circulatory system that moves blood around your body. Heart muscle contracts, but the organ also needs supporting tissues and a lining. Cells themselves contain smaller structures: a membrane controls exchange, and chemical reactions take place inside. Living cells need supplies and must remove wastes.

Why know this?

This helps explain why a problem in one organ can affect distant parts of the body. It also makes microscope pictures meaningful: a tissue sample reveals the small living structures behind the organ’s larger job.

01

One cell can be enough

A bacterium is a whole single-celled organism. It carries out life processes without having a heart, lungs or other organs.

02

A leaf is an organ too

Plants also have specialised cells and tissues. A leaf combines tissues involved in capturing light, exchanging gases and transporting materials.

03

An invisible journey

Oxygen can cross cell membranes by diffusion: its net movement is from higher to lower concentration. Circulating blood brings supplies close to body cells.

THINK / DRAW / TRY

Make it a conversation.

With paper and pencil, draw five frames: a heart muscle cell, heart muscle tissue, a heart, the circulatory system, and a person. Link them with arrows labelled “is part of”. Add a job beneath each frame. In the heart frame, add a lining and supporting tissue. Take turns explaining why simply adding more muscle cells would not replace those jobs.

One more twist

A bacterium has no tissues or organs. Does that mean it is only part of an organism, or could it be a complete living thing?

Help me explain this +

For the opening prediction, squeezing alone is insufficient: a useful pump needs an organised structure, including chambers, a lining and valves that help prevent backflow. Different tissues contribute different properties. Listen for “different jobs working together”, rather than just “more cells”. For the twist, one cell can be a complete organism; the tissue–organ–system ladder describes complex many-celled bodies, not a requirement for all life. The drawing shows levels of organisation, not stages through which one cell grows into a heart. Its frames are not to scale. Cells are active living units, unlike passive building bricks.

A common mix-up

An organ is not one enormous cell. It contains multiple tissue types, each made from cells and often materials those cells produce.

Think like a scientist

Two microscope photographs show cells at different apparent sizes. How could you tell whether the cells really differ in size? Look for scale bars: picture size alone is not a measurement.
